children: A decades-old, antiquated telecommunications system that federal air traffic controllers rely on will continue to have problems until it is properly funded and fully upgraded with modern equipment, according to FAA Administration Bryan Bedford.
"But let's not kid ourselves," he said at a Saturday news conference. "It will continue to break until we fix it."
He added that the transformation from copper to fiber across the ATC network is about 70% complete.
The legacy system is known as the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure
, which is managed by L3Harris Technologies
. Per the company, FTI covers "4,400 facilities, manages more than 29,000 services, and supports the safe operation of 45,000 daily flights across the National Airspace System."
An upgrade from copper wires to fiber that included a router change conducted by L3Harris is to blame for Friday's nationwide ground stop, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy
are working with the FAA on a replacement for FTI. "But in the meantime, until I can build that, I'm stuck with L3Harris, who owns this network."

Bedford maintained that until a new system is completely operational, his agency will continue to maintain the old one. He lamented there isn't enough funding to even do that properly given that a $30B request from Duffy to Congress was reduced first by the House and even more by the Senate.
He noted that ~$12.5B has been spent on modernization efforts so far.
